# {NAME}: a writing framework for agents

## Start

This is a short lesson on {NAME}, a content writing framework for agents. Agents are great at writing code now, but still terrible at copy. {NAME} gets you and your agent to write text the way you write code: decide who reads it and what it should get across, write the tests before the draft, and keep editing until they pass.

If anything you send was drafted with an AI, a post, a deck, an email to a customer, this is for you.

Inkling started with a headline. I asked an AI for the title of a landing page and rejected its tries over and over. Then I wrote one myself in a few minutes: "You don't need an agent sandbox." So I asked the AI why it kept missing, and its answer explained the whole problem.

## Why AI writing fails

The first reason is the root of the others. Code has a judge. When a model writes code, the tests pass or they fail, and training rewarded it for passing, which is why AI got good at code so fast. A headline never fails a test, so the model stops at accurate and complete, and that is a long way from a stranger wanting to click.

With no judge, the model's writing habits come from the rest of its training, and each habit is a problem with a name.

Predictable words. A model predicts the likely next word. Good copy surprises, and a surprise is an unlikely word, so left alone the model drifts to the average of every marketing line it has read, a kind of beige soup.

Trained to concede. The model was trained to be fair and safe, so it concedes, balances and hedges. One rejected headline, "A sandbox runs your agent", hands the competitor the point in four words, when an ad has to take a side.

The curse of context, which psychologists call the curse of knowledge. The model's context is full of what your company built, so it lists features. A good writer thinks like two people at once: a reader who knows nothing about your company, only the general background, and the expert teaching them. That is hard even for humans.

A smaller version is writing from the middle of a conversation. The reader wasn't there, so the first line has to say where they are and why they should care.

Formula punch. The model learned "punchy" as a few shapes, like "it's not this, it's that", and repeats them. A human writer learned punchy from watching people react.

Cramming. The model fits everything in, when good copy cuts to one claim. "You don't need an agent sandbox" says one thing a founder searching for a sandbox didn't expect.

Poor theory of mind. The model rarely asks who is reading and which mind they need: a seller and an engineer for a brochure on a technical product, a lawyer for an order form, an investor for a pitch deck, and often more than one at once.

## The judge prefers the machine

So why not ask another AI to grade the writing? Researchers at Meta tested exactly that this year. They showed AI judges two versions of the same part of a research paper, one written by the expert and one by a model, and asked which was better.

The judges picked the model's version up to 85 percent of the time, and when an AI wrote the grading checklist first, the model won every time. Judges like familiar text, and to a model, model text is the most familiar there is. The judge is grading its own handwriting, so a plain AI grader can't be trusted with writing.

Meta fixed it by tuning the rubric on pairs where the human version should win. We tried something cheaper: a prompt that predicts how I will react, shown lines I approved and lines I threw out. It matched my verdict about four times in five, which beat the tuned rubric on our own writing.

## How {NAME} works

{NAME} turns writing into the same loop as code. You don't have to learn any commands: your AI assistant follows the process and runs the checks on its own draft before you see it.

It starts before the first word. Who reads this, from where, knowing what, and deciding what? And what is the one thing they should take away?

Then come the tests, written first, like code tests. You write what a reader must be able to say afterwards: what this is in one line, the one takeaway, and what they would do next.

Then comes the draft, and along the way your agent can pick up five tools. None of them is required.

The first is a spell-checker for style. It's plain code with no AI in it, so it's free and instant, and it flags em dashes, words like "seamless", hedges, and the "not this but that" shape.

The second is Jev, a small and cheap AI model that answers yes-or-no questions about each line, like "is there a number here with no takeaway?" Each answer costs a fraction of a cent.

The third is a judge that learned from lines I approved and lines I threw out, so it stops siding with the machine.

The fourth, still a prototype, measures surprise. If a reader could finish your sentence for you, the sentence does no work.

The fifth sends in pretend readers: AI models, each given a persona like a busy engineer or a founder who skims, read the draft and answer. If their answers miss your tests, you fix the text.

It runs in two rounds. First a panel: the same readers compare the old and new draft without knowing which is which, and each round's edits get smaller, like tuning a guitar. Then fresh readers who have never seen it read the final draft once. If they get the main points, you stop.

On top sit modes: docs, posts, ads, decks and legal pages. The mode picks which rules run and which readers are in the room.

Images follow the same idea. Every prompt carries a fixed style block, exact counts, every label spelled out, and a style reference with no text in it. Every illustration in this video came from that recipe.

## What we learned

The first day of testing taught us three things.

Introduce yourself. We gave a blog post about long-running agents to readers with zero context. The skimmer said the product names meant nothing to him, because the draft never said what the product was. The model had written it mid-conversation and assumed everyone already knew. The rewrite opens with one plain sentence about the product. Before, the founder persona said it would stop reading halfway; after, it said it would sign up and try it that day.

Credit your sources. Skeptical readers called the post an ad and asked who was paying whom. Naming the public study behind the numbers turned that into "one company's study", a doubt a reader can live with.

Test with realistic readers. Our first readers were told to hunt for doubts, and a reader told to hunt always finds one. Real readers are busy and generous, they know who wrote the piece, and one real source earns their trust. So a test fails only on what would make a real reader stop, and once the core expectations pass, we stop editing. Polishing past that point pushes the copy back toward slop.

## The rules

The rules fit on one screen. First, what good writing does:

- Open on the concrete thing.
- Explain the mechanism before the meaning.
- Name the tool, the file, the error.
- Give every number its consequence.
- Quote the real artifact.
- Make one claim, and lead with what the reader gets.

Then the shapes we ban:

- Em dashes.
- "It wasn't this, it was that."
- "This, not that" at the end of a line.
- Punchlines in threes.
- Stacks of one-line paragraphs.
- Fake epiphanies.
- Keynote closers.
- A vague "most".

The full list is below the video.

## Recap

Agents write weak copy because nothing tells them when it failed. {NAME} gives them that signal. Decide who reads it and what they should take away, write that down as a test before the draft, let readers with no context try it, and stop editing once they get it.
